title: Particle Physics Equipment
alt: The one that sounds like the oracle at the center of the galaxy where the hero travels to hear a prophecy is probably Brookhaven National Laboratory's now-dismantled COSMOTRON.
transcript:
Particle Physics Equipment
By how much it sounds like an offering at a high-end spa in a sci-fi/fantasy novel
[Rightwards arrow with label "more"]
[From left to right, on a line with dense tick-marks arrayed from a solid baseline at the left end and an arrow onwards at the right end:]
[Five items, forming an uneven loose group very close to the left end of the scale:] Geiger counter
Cherenkov detector
Photomultiplier tube
Linear accelerator
Scintillation counter
[About 20% from the left edge:] Ion chamber
[About 25% from the left edge:] Cyclotron
[The next two items are almost touching, far to the right end of the extant scale, a large empty gap of nothing but tickmarks between the last item and these:] Bubble Chamber
Cloud Chamber
explanation:
The comic rates various equipment used in particle physics by how much the name sounds like an offering at a sci-fi spa. Some things, like a , are very hard to interpret in this way, whereas  others, such as s, are very easy to imagine as spa equipment.


 

Position  	Device	Actual use                                                                                                                                                                                 	Spa interpretation
2         	      	Measures ionizing radiation. It's the source of the iconic clicking sound that gets faster if there is more radiation. Geiger counters were the subject of 2607: Geiger Counter.           	As Geiger counters are well-known devices, it's unlikely that anyone would use this term to describe anything at a sci-fi spa, unless that spa was worried about radiation.
3         	      	Detects the  emitted when particles are moving faster than the speed of light for the medium they're in. The radiation is primarily in the ultraviolet, but human eyes perceive it as blue.	Detectors are not commonly considered related to spas or relaxation.
4         	      	A very sensitive light detector                                                                                                                                                            	Sounds like it could perhaps be a fancy word for a tanning booth, or a replacement part used in one, but this clunky term would not be advertised to the public.
6         	      	A straight-line particle accelerator                                                                                                                                                       	A lot of spa treatments are aimed at getting rid of lines, particularly on the face, so this sounds like it would be counter-productive at a spa.
7         	      	Measures the number of particles which generate light when hitting certain materials.                                                                                                      	This sounds like it might be similar to a nail or makeup counter, where you could have treatments applied to make you sparkle (although Randall has given it a surprisingly low rating considering that this sounds quite appealing).
13        	      	Measures the amount of ions created by ionizing radiation; commonly found in smoke detectors.                                                                                              	Reference to ions calls to mind  often used when advertising beauty products to make them sound more impressive than they actually are.
18        	      	A type of circular particle accelerator. Can be used in cancer treatment, but this would not normally be done in a spa.                                                                    	In popular culture, adding '-tron' to the end of a machine name is often used to signify science that is sufficiently advanced as to be indistinguishable from magic. Some beauty treatments are applied in cycles (in particular, 'skin cycling'), so a cyclotron  may sound like a highly-advanced shortcut to those same results.
71        	      	A big bowl of a fluid, usually liquid hydrogen, that can detect electrically charged particles moving through it.                                                                          	It sounds like a , a feature commonly found in spas.
72        	      	A transparent container containing supersaturated water or alcohol, which reacts to ionizing radiation.                                                                                    	Clouds are often associated with softness, luxury, and pleasurable feelings (e.g., being on cloud nine), so this may sound like something it would be nice to relax in.
Title text	      	A proton synchrotron ring used from the early 1950s to 1966. The name comes from cosmic rays, which it partially reproduced.                                                               	
The suffix "" is often used to denote some technical device. Such naming was especially popular in 1960s, both in real devices (cyclotron, Cosmotron) as well as in science fictional machines of openly stated purpose but  operation, and since then being more .

The stem "cosmo-" can also be associated with power and magic, which is about right for an oracle, in addition to being a well known prefix for , and so might well invoke fantasy-inclined concepts as well as the .
